newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS - Greece to raise 280 bln drachmas in new taxes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Greece to raise 280 bln drachmas in new taxes.

text.p: Greece will use a one-two punch of eliminating tax breaks while imposing new levies, mostly on the affluent, to raise 280 billion drachmas ($1.17 billion) in revenues next year, National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou said on Tuesday.
Special tax breaks will be cut across the board while new taxes will be imposed on those with large holdings of property or financial assets, he told reporters.
"We are abolishing tax breaks that have no social or growth character. We aren't touching small incomes," he told a news conference while presenting the draft tax bill.
Papandoniou has said he will unveil the toughest budget in 15 years on Friday to push Greece closer to the strict targets set out for joining European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Greece is the only EU member which has failed to meet any of the economic criteria for joining the EMU and acknowledged last week that its best hope was to be in a second tier of countries, aiming to join a year or two late in 2000 or 2001.
Papandoniou, who will submit the tax measures in a draft bill to parliament, said about 130 billion drachmas will come from abolishing tax breaks and 150 billion from new taxes.
In the run-up to the budget, he has said putting Greece's economic house in order was crucial and he would slash state spending, limit state hiring and speed privatisation.

The tax bill confirmed leaks and announcements that interest from state securities issued after January 1 will be taxed at 7.5 percent, return from derivatives at 15 percent, capital gains from share transactions of non-listed firms at 20 percent.
Budget and tax measures announced in recent days are the first programme put together by socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis, elected to a four-year term in September.
Simitis, who took over from the late socialist party founder Andreas Papandreou in January, has said economic responsibility was vital to being taken seriously by EU partners.

Papandoniou also confirmed that assets of mutual funds and investment companies will be taxed at a 0.2 percent rate, the corporate tax rate of bank profits will rise to 40 percent from 35 percent and prepayment of tax by banks will be raised to 60 percent from 50 percent currently.

Real estate will be taxed according to a scale, with tax exemption of holdings set at 60 million drachmas of their objective value for each person or corporation and 150 million for a four member family. Agricultural property is not taxed.

Among the special interest tax breaks that will be abolished are those for parliamentarians and journalists. People earning more than 15 million drachmas a year will no longer be able to deduct medical expenses.

There will be a gradual phase out of tax exemptions for sailors and pilots, said Papandoniou. He gave no reason for the preferential treatment but it seemed aimed at an effort to head off strikes in the transportation sector.

Bonuses for Greece's legion of civil servants will also be taxed for the first time at a 15 percent rate as well as foreign exchange deposits made by residents and interbank deposits, said Papandoniou. He gave no rate for the latter.
Papandoniou's measures are part of a package to reduce the budget deficit to 4.2 percent of GDP in 1997 from an expected 7.6 percent in 1996. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4 ($1=240.3 Drachma)
